subparts.text: Define database, DBMS and database system.
subparts.answer: A database is an organised collection of related data. A DBMS is software that creates, stores, manages and controls access to a database. A database system is the database, DBMS, application programs, people, procedures and hardware working together.

subparts.text: State FOUR limitations of the file-based approach that a DBMS addresses.
subparts.answer: The limitations include data redundancy, data inconsistency, difficult data sharing, weak concurrency control, limited security, program-data dependence, and difficult backup and recovery.

subparts.text: Nusantara Learning Hub still keeps its customer records in a spreadsheet program. Table 1 shows a sample of the data. Study Table 1 and answer the following.

children.text: Identify TWO candidate keys and ONE primary key from Table 1. Give ONE reason for your chosen primary key.
children.answer: Candidate keys: Customer No, Customer IC and e-mail (any TWO). Primary key: Customer No, because it is unique for every row and does not change.

children.text: Explain why the spreadsheet in Table 1 is not a substitute for a database.
children.answer: A spreadsheet stores unrelated copies of data, so the same customer can be repeated and updated inconsistently. It lacks integrity constraints, concurrency control, access control and recovery facilities that a DBMS provides.

questions.answer:
a) A database is an organised collection of related data. A DBMS is software that creates, stores, manages and controls access to a database. A database system is the database, DBMS, application programs, people, procedures and hardware working together.

b) The limitations include data redundancy, data inconsistency, difficult data sharing, weak concurrency control, limited security, program-data dependence, and difficult backup and recovery.

c i) Candidate keys: Customer No, Customer IC and e-mail (any TWO). Primary key: Customer No, because it is unique for every row and does not change.

c ii) A spreadsheet stores unrelated copies of data, so the same customer can be repeated and updated inconsistently. It lacks integrity constraints, concurrency control, access control and recovery facilities that a DBMS provides.

questions.source: ICT200/ICT450 KB Topic 3 Relational Data Model

subparts.text: Nusantara University keeps its student and course records in the tables shown below. Table 1 shows the STUDENT table and Table 2 shows the COURSE table. Identify the primary key of each table and TWO candidate keys in the STUDENT table.
subparts.answer: STUDENT: primary key Student_ID; candidate keys Student_IC, Student_ID and EMAIL. COURSE: primary key COURSE_ID.

subparts.text: Explain entity integrity and referential integrity. Give ONE example from Table 1 and Table 2.
subparts.answer: Entity integrity: a primary-key column cannot contain a null or duplicate value. Referential integrity: a foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value or be null. Example: every COURSE_ID in STUDENT must exist in COURSE, and STUDENT_ID must be unique and not null.

subparts.text: Define tuple, attribute, degree and cardinality.
subparts.answer: Tuple = a row; attribute = a column; degree = number of attributes; cardinality = number of tuples.

subparts.text: Explain TWO update anomalies that can occur in the STUDENT table if course details are stored together with student details.
subparts.answer: If COURSE_NAME is repeated for every student, changing a course name in one row but not the others causes an update anomaly. Deleting the last student for a course loses the course data (delete anomaly), and adding a new course before any student enrols is difficult (insert anomaly).

questions.answer:
a) STUDENT: primary key Student_ID; candidate keys Student_IC, Student_ID and EMAIL. COURSE: primary key COURSE_ID.

b) Entity integrity: a primary-key column cannot contain a null or duplicate value. Referential integrity: a foreign-key value must match an existing primary-key value or be null. Example: every COURSE_ID in STUDENT must exist in COURSE, and STUDENT_ID must be unique and not null.

c) Tuple = a row; attribute = a column; degree = number of attributes; cardinality = number of tuples.

d) If COURSE_NAME is repeated for every student, changing a course name in one row but not the others causes an update anomaly. Deleting the last student for a course loses the course data (delete anomaly), and adding a new course before any student enrols is difficult (insert anomaly).

subparts.text: Figure 1 shows part of an ERD for a supplier and product database. Identify the entities, their attributes, the relationship between them and the cardinalities shown.
subparts.answer: Entities: VENDOR with VEND_CODE, VEND_CONTACT, VEND_AREACODE and VEND_PHONE; PRODUCT with PROD_CODE, PROD_DESCRIPT, PROD_PRICE, PROD_ON_HAND and VEND_CODE. Relationship: VENDOR supplies PRODUCT. Cardinality: one VENDOR supplies many PRODUCTs (1:M).

subparts.text: Explain the referential integrity constraint shown in Figure 1. Give ONE example of an operation that would violate it.
subparts.answer: PRODUCT.VEND_CODE is a foreign key that must match an existing VENDOR.VEND_CODE or be null. Inserting a PRODUCT with a VEND_CODE that does not exist in VENDOR violates referential integrity; deleting a VENDOR that still has PRODUCTs also violates it unless the products are deleted or reassigned.

subparts.text: Map the ERD in Figure 1 to a relational schema. Mark the primary key and foreign key.
subparts.answer: VENDOR(VEND_CODE PK, VEND_CONTACT, VEND_AREACODE, VEND_PHONE); PRODUCT(PROD_CODE PK, PROD_DESCRIPT, PROD_PRICE, PROD_ON_HAND, VEND_CODE FK REFERENCES VENDOR(VEND_CODE)).
marking_points: PRODUCT relation, primary key and foreign key (3)

questions.answer:
a) Entities: VENDOR with VEND_CODE, VEND_CONTACT, VEND_AREACODE and VEND_PHONE; PRODUCT with PROD_CODE, PROD_DESCRIPT, PROD_PRICE, PROD_ON_HAND and VEND_CODE. Relationship: VENDOR supplies PRODUCT. Cardinality: one VENDOR supplies many PRODUCTs (1:M).

b) PRODUCT.VEND_CODE is a foreign key that must match an existing VENDOR.VEND_CODE or be null. Inserting a PRODUCT with a VEND_CODE that does not exist in VENDOR violates referential integrity; deleting a VENDOR that still has PRODUCTs also violates it unless the products are deleted or reassigned.

c) VENDOR(VEND_CODE PK, VEND_CONTACT, VEND_AREACODE, VEND_PHONE); PRODUCT(PROD_CODE PK, PROD_DESCRIPT, PROD_PRICE, PROD_ON_HAND, VEND_CODE FK REFERENCES VENDOR(VEND_CODE)).

subparts.text: The spreadsheet in Table 1 shows course and student records for a college. Study Table 1 and identify the candidate key and all functional dependencies.
subparts.answer: Relation: COURSE_RECORD(CourseCode, CourseName, TutorID, TutorName, StudentID, StudentName, DOB, Gender, LastAttendance). Candidate key: (CourseCode, StudentID). FDs: CourseCode -> CourseName, TutorID, TutorName; StudentID -> StudentName, DOB, Gender; (CourseCode, StudentID) -> LastAttendance.

1NF: all attributes are atomic. 2NF: 1NF and every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole candidate key. 3NF: 2NF and no non-key attribute is transitively dependent on the key.

subparts.text: Identify the partial and transitive dependencies in Table 1.
subparts.answer: Partial: CourseCode -> CourseName, TutorID, TutorName depends on part of the key; StudentID -> StudentName, DOB, Gender depends on part of the key. Transitive: CourseCode -> TutorID -> TutorName.

subparts.text: Decompose Table 1 into 3NF relations. Show the primary and foreign keys.
subparts.answer: COURSE(CourseCode PK, CourseName, TutorID FK); TUTOR(TutorID PK, TutorName); STUDENT(StudentID PK, StudentName, DOB, Gender); ATTENDANCE(CourseCode PK, StudentID PK, LastAttendance, FKs to COURSE and STUDENT).

questions.answer:
a) Relation: COURSE_RECORD(CourseCode, CourseName, TutorID, TutorName, StudentID, StudentName, DOB, Gender, LastAttendance). Candidate key: (CourseCode, StudentID). FDs: CourseCode -> CourseName, TutorID, TutorName; StudentID -> StudentName, DOB, Gender; (CourseCode, StudentID) -> LastAttendance.

b) 1NF: all attributes are atomic. 2NF: 1NF and every non-key attribute is fully functionally dependent on the whole candidate key. 3NF: 2NF and no non-key attribute is transitively dependent on the key.

c) Partial: CourseCode -> CourseName, TutorID, TutorName depends on part of the key; StudentID -> StudentName, DOB, Gender depends on part of the key. Transitive: CourseCode -> TutorID -> TutorName.

d) COURSE(CourseCode PK, CourseName, TutorID FK); TUTOR(TutorID PK, TutorName); STUDENT(StudentID PK, StudentName, DOB, Gender); ATTENDANCE(CourseCode PK, StudentID PK, LastAttendance, FKs to COURSE and STUDENT).

subparts.text: Figure 1 shows the database design process. Explain FOUR activities carried out during the database design phase.
subparts.answer: Conceptual design: identify entities, attributes and relationships and build a conceptual model. Logical design: map the conceptual model to a relational schema, choose keys and normalize. Physical design: choose storage structures, indexes, file organisation and access paths. Implementation: create the database objects and load the data.

subparts.text: Differentiate the SDLC and the DBLC.
subparts.answer: SDLC covers the whole information-system life cycle; DBLC focuses on the database component within that system and runs through its own design, implementation, testing, operation and maintenance phases.

subparts.text: Compare top-down and bottom-up database design.
subparts.answer: Top-down starts from the overall data model and breaks it into components. Bottom-up starts from individual data elements and combines them into a model.
Centralized design is controlled by one design team or location. Decentralized design distributes design work across teams or locations and requires reconciliation.
